## Lithosphere and Plate Motion
Try first: before reading on, write down what you think the lithosphere is made of and what lies beneath it. Then check your answer against the next paragraph. The lithosphere is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates that float on the ductile asthenosphere. The plates themselves are rigid, but the layer beneath them flows slowly, which is precisely what allows the plates to ride upon it. Three mechanisms drive plate motion: mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push.
Retrieval check: name the three driving mechanisms from memory before continuing. Try first: estimate the units in which relative plate motion is measured, and justify your estimate. Then read the correction below. Relative motion between plates is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹). A common wrong idea is that plates move at metres per year; the material states centimetres, so that idea fails by a factor of roughly one hundred. The rate is slow, yet over millions of years it accumulates into large distances.
Why it matters: interpreting geodetic and seismic data correctly depends on using the stated units; an order-of-magnitude error changes every prediction built on them. Try first: sketch, from memory, the three boundary types and the earthquake style each produces. Then compare your sketch with the table below. Boundary type controls earthquake style. The correspondence is exact:
| Boundary type | Relative motion | Typical seismic style | |---|---|---| | Divergent | Plates pull apart | Normal-fault earthquakes, shallow depths | | Convergent | Plates collide | Thrust-fault earthquakes, deep to shallow | | Transform | Plates slide past | Strike-slip earthquakes, shallow to intermediate | Retrieval check: which boundary type produces thrust-fault earthquakes, and over what depth range? Try first: propose as many reasons as you can for why earthquakes cluster at boundaries rather than occurring randomly. Then read the four reasons the material gives. Earthquakes cluster at boundaries for four reasons. First, stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, and strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Second, fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. Third, rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. Fourth, geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
The clustering mechanism as a chain: edges locked by friction → strain builds → exceeds rock strength → slip (earthquake). Try first: state, in one sentence, what a map of global earthquakes represents. Then check it against the key point. Key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. A map of earthquakes is therefore effectively a map of plate boundaries.
